1.description: Male Ashe junipers releasing massive clouds of pollen, triggering cedar fever across central Texas
1.childFriendlyNote: Shake a branch and a yellow cloud puffs out like smoke. That's tree dust called pollen flying everywhere!

1.description: Cardinals bright against bare winter branches, males beginning to sing territorial songs on mild mornings
1.childFriendlyNote: A bright red bird sits on a bare branch like a little Christmas ornament and whistles "cheer-cheer-cheer!"

1.description: Armadillos foraging on mild winter evenings, rooting through leaf litter for grubs and insects
1.childFriendlyNote: A little armoured animal shuffles through leaves at dusk, snuffling and digging like a tiny tank looking for bugs

1.description: Large flocks of wintering robins gathering in trees with persistent berries, especially hollies and hackberries
1.childFriendlyNote: Hundreds of round red-bellied birds huddle in berry trees like a feathery picnic party

1.description: Flocks of cedar waxwings stripping berries from hollies and junipers, their thin high-pitched calls overhead
1.childFriendlyNote: Masked birds with fancy yellow tail-tips gobble berries and pass them beak-to-beak like sharing sweets

1.description: Live oaks standing green and full through winter, their broad spreading canopies unchanged by cold
1.childFriendlyNote: While other trees are bare and sleeping, the live oak keeps all its dark green leaves like a stubborn friend who won't go to bed

2.description: Cedar fever continues as Ashe juniper pollen counts soar on windy days across the Hill Country
2.childFriendlyNote: The juniper trees are still puffing golden clouds. If you look at the hills on a windy day they look smoky!

2.description: Male cardinals singing from fence posts and treetops, establishing territories for the coming nesting season
2.childFriendlyNote: The bright red cardinal sits on the tallest branch and sings "birdy-birdy-birdy" to tell everyone this is his garden

2.description: Great blue herons standing motionless at pond edges and creek banks, hunting fish in the winter quiet
2.childFriendlyNote: A tall grey-blue bird stands perfectly still by the water like a statue. Then snap! It grabs a fish!

2.description: Cedar waxwing flocks moving between fruiting trees, their soft trilling calls filling the cold air
2.childFriendlyNote: A whole flock of sleek birds with black masks swoops into a tree and eats every single berry before flying on

2.description: Mockingbirds defending winter berry territories, flashing white wing patches at intruders
2.childFriendlyNote: This grey bird is the best copycat. It can sing like a cardinal, a blue jay, even a car alarm!

3.description: Peak cedar fever season, pollen counts among the highest of the year on dry windy days
3.childFriendlyNote: The juniper trees are still making so much yellow dust that cars turn greenish-yellow overnight!

3.description: Massive robin flocks foraging in lawns and fields, sometimes thousands together in winter roosts
3.childFriendlyNote: Robins hop across the playground tugging worms out of the ground, tug, tug, pop! Dinner time!

3.description: Red-tailed hawks soaring over highways and open fields, their raspy screaming call echoing across the sky
3.childFriendlyNote: A big brown hawk circles high up making that wild screaming call. It can spot a mouse from way up there!

3.description: Bats roosting in caves and under bridges through winter, mostly inactive during cold spells
3.childFriendlyNote: Thousands of bats snuggle together under bridges and in caves, staying warm and waiting for bug season

3.description: Sandhill cranes wintering in agricultural fields and wetlands, their rattling bugle calls carrying far
3.childFriendlyNote: Tall grey birds with red caps dance and trumpet in the fields. They sound like rusty gates swinging open!

4.description: Cedar pollen season beginning to wane but still significant on warm dry days
4.childFriendlyNote: The juniper pollen clouds are finally calming down, less yellow dust on everything!

4.description: Cardinals singing more frequently as days lengthen, pairs beginning to form
4.childFriendlyNote: Mr and Mrs Cardinal are singing love songs to each other. He's bright red and she's a warm golden brown

4.description: Green anoles emerging on warm afternoons to bask on sunny walls and fence posts
4.childFriendlyNote: A bright green lizard does push-ups on the fence to warm up in the sunshine. Look how it puffs out a pink throat bubble!

4.description: Sandhill cranes still wintering in Texas fields, beginning to get restless before spring migration
4.childFriendlyNote: The big grey cranes are still here, honking and dancing, but soon they'll fly all the way north!

4.description: Elbow bush among the first native shrubs to bloom, tiny yellow flowers on bare zigzag branches
4.childFriendlyNote: This funny zigzag bush is one of the first to wake up. Little yellow flowers pop out on its bare bendy branches

4.description: Cedar waxwings continuing to feast on winter berries in large chattering flocks
4.childFriendlyNote: The fancy masked birds are still here gobbling berries. They eat so many they sometimes get a bit wobbly!

5.description: Cedar pollen season winding down, last significant releases on windy days
5.childFriendlyNote: The sneezy juniper trees are almost done making pollen. Relief is coming!

5.description: First redbud flower buds swelling on bare branches, earliest blooms possible in southern areas
5.childFriendlyNote: Tiny pink buds are swelling on bare branches. Soon the whole tree will look like it's covered in pink butterflies!

5.description: Mockingbirds beginning to expand their song repertoire, practicing new phrases for breeding season
5.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird is practising new songs. Count how many different sounds it makes in a row!

5.description: Sandhill cranes beginning northward migration, large flocks forming overhead
5.childFriendlyNote: Look up. Hundreds of grey cranes spiral into the sky like a feathered tornado, heading north for summer!

5.description: Great horned owls already nesting and incubating eggs, their deep hooting echoes at dusk
5.childFriendlyNote: "Hoo-hoo-hoooo". A big owl with ear tufts is already sitting on eggs in the cold, keeping them warm with fluffy feathers

5.description: Green anoles basking on warm afternoons, beginning to turn from winter brown back to green
5.childFriendlyNote: The little lizards are changing colour from brown back to bright green, like living mood rings on the fence!

6.description: Redbuds beginning to open their magenta-pink blossoms on bare branches across central Texas
6.childFriendlyNote: The bare trees are sprouting bright pink flowers right out of their bark. No leaves needed!

6.description: Carolina wrens singing their loud "teakettle-teakettle" from brush piles and garden corners
6.childFriendlyNote: A tiny rusty-brown bird with a big white eyebrow shouts "teakettle-teakettle-teakettle!" so loud you jump!

6.description: Great horned owl chicks hatching, parents hunting extra prey to feed fuzzy white nestlings
6.childFriendlyNote: Fluffy white owl babies have hatched. They look like cotton balls with big eyes sitting in the nest!

6.description: Green anoles increasingly active on warm days, males displaying bright pink dewlaps
6.childFriendlyNote: The boy lizards puff out a bubblegum-pink flap under their chin and do push-ups to show off!

6.description: First gulf fritillary butterflies appearing on warm days, bright orange with silver-spotted underwings
6.childFriendlyNote: A bright orange butterfly with secret silver sparkles under its wings floats through the garden

7.description: Redbuds in full bloom along roadsides and woodland edges, pink-purple flowers covering bare branches
7.childFriendlyNote: Whole trees glow pink like cotton candy lollipops. The flowers grow straight out of the branches and even the trunk!

7.description: Texas mountain laurel flower buds swelling, first purple clusters beginning to open with grape-soda scent
7.childFriendlyNote: Sniff the purple flower clusters on this evergreen tree. They smell exactly like grape bubblegum!

7.description: Mockingbirds in full song, sometimes singing through the night under streetlights
7.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird sings all night long under the streetlight. It knows more than 200 different songs!

7.description: Carolina wrens building nests in porch corners, flower pots, and any sheltered nook
7.childFriendlyNote: Check your boots on the porch. A cheeky little wren might be building a nest in there!

7.description: Green anoles fully active now, males doing territorial push-up displays on fences and walls
7.childFriendlyNote: The green lizard does push-ups on the wall and flashes its pink chin flap: "This is my fence!"

7.description: Henbit carpeting lawns and fields with tiny purple flowers, one of the earliest spring wildflowers
7.childFriendlyNote: Lawns turn purple with millions of tiny flowers. Get close and they look like little dragon mouths!

8.description: Texas mountain laurel in peak bloom, heavy purple flower clusters dangling and filling the air with grape-soda fragrance
8.childFriendlyNote: Close your eyes and sniff. It smells like someone opened a grape soda! Those are the purple mountain laurel flowers

8.description: Redbuds at peak bloom, heart-shaped leaves beginning to emerge behind the flowers
8.childFriendlyNote: The pink redbud trees are at their prettiest, and look, tiny heart-shaped leaves are starting to unfold behind the flowers!

8.description: Bluebonnet rosettes growing rapidly in fields and roadsides, flower stalks just beginning to push up
8.childFriendlyNote: Flat circles of fuzzy green leaves are getting ready for the biggest flower show in Texas. The bluebonnets are coming!

8.description: Robin winter flocks beginning to break up as some birds start migrating north
8.childFriendlyNote: The big robin flocks are breaking up. Some are heading north, but a few will stay and sing for us

8.description: Painted lady butterflies beginning their northward migration through Texas, orange and black wings flashing
8.childFriendlyNote: Orange butterflies with painted spots are passing through on an incredible journey north. Wave them on!

9.description: First bluebonnet flowers opening in southern areas, blue spikes rising from fuzzy rosettes along highways
9.childFriendlyNote: The first blue flowers are popping up like tiny bonnets. Soon there will be millions turning whole fields blue!

9.description: Mountain laurel still blooming strongly, purple wisteria-like clusters fragrant in warm afternoons
9.childFriendlyNote: Take a big sniff near the purple flowers, grape soda smell! The bees love it too

9.description: Redbud flowers fading as heart-shaped leaves expand, pink petals drifting down like confetti
9.childFriendlyNote: Pink petals are falling like confetti and cute heart-shaped leaves are taking their place!

9.description: Mexican plum trees covered in clusters of fragrant white blossoms, attracting early pollinators
9.childFriendlyNote: White fluffy blossoms cover the plum tree like a cloud and smell so sweet that bees come buzzing from everywhere

9.description: First scissor-tailed flycatchers returning from Central America, their spectacular long tails streaming behind
9.childFriendlyNote: A pale pink bird with a tail twice as long as its body lands on a wire. It looks like it's trailing ribbons!

9.description: Green anoles fully active, males displaying pink dewlaps and chasing rivals across garden walls
9.childFriendlyNote: Lizard wrestling! Two green anoles chase each other around the tree trunk, flashing their pink chin fans

10.description: Bluebonnets spreading across fields and highway medians, blue carpets intensifying daily
10.childFriendlyNote: Fields are turning blue like the sky fell down! Get close and the flowers smell sweet like grape honey

10.description: Indian paintbrush lighting up roadsides with scarlet-orange tips among the bluebonnets
10.childFriendlyNote: Red-orange flowers pop up in the bluebonnets like someone dipped paintbrushes in bright paint and stuck them in the ground!

10.description: Spring monarch migration beginning through Texas, butterflies heading north from Mexico
10.childFriendlyNote: Orange and black monarchs are flying through on an amazing journey. They came all the way from mountains in Mexico!

10.description: Scissor-tailed flycatchers arriving on fence lines and power wires, long tail feathers scissoring in flight
10.childFriendlyNote: The Oklahoma state bird is back! Watch it fly off the wire and its long tail opens and closes like scissors, snip!

10.description: Mountain laurel blossoms fading, last sweet grape-soda fragrance of the season
10.childFriendlyNote: The purple grape-soda flowers are dropping their petals. Quick, get one last sniff before they're gone!

10.description: Prickly pear cacti pushing out bright green new pads, soft and spineless at first
10.childFriendlyNote: Baby cactus pads are sprouting. They're neon green and weirdly soft, like little rubbery ears (but don't touch, spines are coming!)

11.description: Bluebonnet fields at their most spectacular, entire hillsides painted deep blue
11.childFriendlyNote: Whole hills look like blue oceans swaying in the breeze. This is the best week for bluebonnets!

11.description: Indian paintbrush at peak, mixing scarlet splashes among blue and gold wildflowers
11.childFriendlyNote: The red paintbrush flowers blaze among the blue like little campfires in a blue sea!

11.description: Monarchs passing through Texas, females stopping to lay eggs on milkweed sprouting in fields
11.childFriendlyNote: The mama monarchs are stopping to lay teeny eggs on milkweed. Each egg is smaller than a grain of rice!

11.description: Scissor-tailed flycatchers establishing territories, spectacular sky-dancing courtship flights
11.childFriendlyNote: The scissor-tail zooms up high, tumbles and twists with its long tail streaming. It's a sky dance to impress a girlfriend!

11.description: First ruby-throated hummingbirds arriving from across the Gulf of Mexico, exhausted and hungry
11.childFriendlyNote: Tiny buzzing jewel-birds are arriving after flying non-stop across the whole Gulf of Mexico. Put out sugar water, they're starving!

12.description: Bluebonnets at absolute peak across central Texas, families stopping for photos in the fields
12.childFriendlyNote: It's bluebonnet picture time! Sit gently in the flowers and look up. You're in a sea of blue with white tips like tiny bonnets

12.description: Indian paintbrush blazing alongside bluebonnets, the classic red-and-blue Texas wildflower combo
12.childFriendlyNote: Red and blue side by side. Nature made its own patriotic painting in the meadow!

12.description: Monarch migration in full swing through Texas, nectaring on wildflowers and laying eggs on milkweed
12.childFriendlyNote: Follow a monarch with your eyes. Watch it dip its curly tongue into each flower like a tiny straw!

12.description: Live oaks dropping old leaves while new lime-green leaves emerge simultaneously, catkins shedding pollen
12.childFriendlyNote: The live oak is doing something wild, dropping old brown leaves and growing fresh green ones at the same time!

12.description: Ruby-throated hummingbirds arriving in numbers, males flashing iridescent red throats in sunlight
12.childFriendlyNote: A tiny bird hovers like a helicopter. Turn your head and its throat flashes from black to blazing ruby red!

12.description: Green anoles very active, territorial males bobbing heads and displaying dewlaps on every warm surface
12.childFriendlyNote: Anoles are everywhere now, doing push-ups on trees, fences, walls, even your windowsill!

13.description: Bluebonnets beginning to fade in southern areas, still peak in northern Hill Country
13.childFriendlyNote: Some bluebonnets are making seed pods now. The flowers turn pink then droop, but there are still blue fields up north!

13.description: First painted buntings arriving, males dazzling with their rainbow plumage of blue, green, and red
13.childFriendlyNote: The most colourful bird in America just arrived. It's painted blue, green, red and yellow like a flying rainbow!

13.description: Monarch spring migration continuing, caterpillars hatching on Texas milkweed plants
13.childFriendlyNote: Check the milkweed for stripy caterpillars: black, yellow and white! They munch leaves all day long

13.description: Scissor-tails nesting on utility poles and in open trees, long tails trailing as they hawk insects
13.childFriendlyNote: Watch the scissor-tail launch off the wire. It grabs a bug mid-air and its tail opens like scissors! Snip-snap!

13.description: Dewberry vines blooming with white flowers along fences and field edges, fruit beginning to form
13.childFriendlyNote: White flowers on thorny vines by the fence are going to turn into the yummiest little wild blackberries soon!

13.description: Ruby-throated hummingbirds established, aggressively defending flower patches and feeders
13.childFriendlyNote: The hummingbird zooms at other birds like a tiny fighter jet: buzz off, these flowers are mine!

14.description: Bluebonnets fading across most areas, seed pods rattling on dried stems
14.childFriendlyNote: Shake a bluebonnet stem. Hear the seeds rattle? They're getting ready to plant themselves for next year!

14.description: Painted buntings singing from treetops, males displaying iridescent plumage in morning light
14.childFriendlyNote: The rainbow bird sings a sweet warbling song from the highest branch so everyone can see how gorgeous he is

14.description: Live oak leaf exchange nearly complete, fresh bright green canopy replacing old leaves, pollen heavy
14.childFriendlyNote: The live oaks are finally done swapping leaves. Everything is fresh bright green and the brown leaf rain is stopping!

14.description: Dewberries forming green fruit, some early berries turning red along sunny fence lines
14.childFriendlyNote: The dewberry flowers are turning into tiny hard green berries. Don't eat them yet, they need to turn dark purple!

14.description: Black-chinned hummingbirds arriving in central and western Texas, joining ruby-throats at feeders
14.childFriendlyNote: Another tiny hummingbird has arrived. This one has a purple stripe that only shows when the light hits just right!

14.description: Texas spiny lizards sunning on fence posts and tree trunks, males doing push-up territorial displays
14.childFriendlyNote: A bumpy grey lizard as long as your hand does push-ups on the fence. Look at the blue patches on his belly!

15.description: Painted buntings nesting in thick brush, males singing territorial songs from exposed perches
15.childFriendlyNote: The rainbow bird is building a secret nest deep in the bushes while the colourful dad sings from up high

15.description: Dewberries ripening to dark purple-black, sweet and juicy along fence rows and woodland edges
15.childFriendlyNote: The dewberries are dark and squishy-ripe! Pop one in your mouth, sweet and purple and juicy (watch the thorns!)

15.description: Scissor-tailed flycatchers incubating eggs, pairs defending nest territories aggressively
15.childFriendlyNote: Mama scissor-tail sits on her eggs while papa chases away any bird that comes too close, even hawks!

15.description: Mexican free-tailed bat colonies growing under bridges, evening flights becoming more spectacular
15.childFriendlyNote: Stand on the bridge at sunset. Thousands of bats pour out like a dark river flowing into the sky!

15.description: Native coral honeysuckle in full bloom, tubular red flowers attracting hummingbirds
15.childFriendlyNote: Red tube-shaped flowers hang in clusters. Pull one off gently and sip the tiny drop of honey-sweet nectar inside!

16.description: Prickly pear flower buds forming on pad edges, yellow-orange blossoms beginning to open
16.childFriendlyNote: The spiky cactus is growing beautiful yellow flowers on its edges. Nature's way of putting a bow on a cactus!

16.description: Black-chinned hummingbirds nesting, building tiny lichen-covered nests on tree branches
16.childFriendlyNote: The hummingbird's nest is the size of a walnut shell! She glues it together with spider silk, so tiny and perfect

16.description: Painted buntings on eggs, females nearly invisible in their olive-green plumage
16.childFriendlyNote: The mama painted bunting is all green. She's hiding on the nest so no one can find her babies!

16.description: Great-tailed grackles nesting in parking lot trees, males puffing up and making outrageous mechanical sounds
16.childFriendlyNote: Shiny purple-black birds in the parking lot make the weirdest sounds: clicks, whistles, rusty gates, and laser beams!

16.description: Bat colonies swelling as pregnant females arrive, evening emergences growing larger
16.childFriendlyNote: The mama bats are arriving. Soon each one will have a tiny pink baby bat clinging to her fur!

16.description: Carolina wren chicks fledging from first broods, noisy families exploring gardens
16.childFriendlyNote: Baby wrens hop out of the nest for the first time, cheeping and fluttering and following mum everywhere!

17.description: Prickly pear in spectacular bloom, large waxy yellow and orange flowers covering the pads
17.childFriendlyNote: The prickly cactus is wearing a crown of bright yellow flowers. Each one is as big as your palm!

17.description: Monarch caterpillars feeding on milkweed, first generation chrysalises forming
17.childFriendlyNote: The stripy caterpillar hangs upside-down and makes a jade-green sleeping bag with gold dots. It's becoming a butterfly inside!

17.description: Ruby-throated hummingbirds nesting, females sitting on two jelly-bean-sized eggs
17.childFriendlyNote: Two eggs the size of jelly beans sit in a walnut-shell nest. Each one will become a buzzing hummingbird!

17.description: Green anoles mating, females beginning to lay single eggs in moist soil and leaf litter
17.childFriendlyNote: The mama lizard hides a tiny white egg under a leaf. It's so small you could mistake it for a pebble!

17.description: First fireflies of the season blinking in eastern Texas yards and meadows at dusk
17.childFriendlyNote: Little lights blink on and off in the grass at twilight. Fireflies are bugs with glow-in-the-dark bottoms!

18.description: Prickly pear bloom continuing, bees buzzing inside the large cup-shaped flowers
18.childFriendlyNote: Peek inside a cactus flower. A fuzzy bee is rolling around in yellow pollen like a tiny dog in a ball pit!

18.description: Bat colonies at near-peak numbers, spectacular sunset emergences from bridges and caves
18.childFriendlyNote: A million bats stream out from under the bridge at sunset. The ribbon of bats stretches across the whole sky!

18.description: Fireflies increasing in number across eastern Texas, blinking yellow-green in warm humid evenings
18.childFriendlyNote: More and more fireflies are joining the light show. The yard looks like it's full of floating stars!

18.description: Grackle chicks fledging, noisy juveniles begging for food in parking lots and picnic areas
18.childFriendlyNote: Baby grackles follow their parents going "cheee cheee cheee" with their mouths wide open, so demanding!

18.description: Box turtles active after spring rains, crossing roads and foraging in woodland leaf litter
18.childFriendlyNote: A turtle with an orange and brown shell walks slowly through the leaves. If scared it pulls everything inside and shuts the door!

18.description: Horsemint beginning to bloom in meadows and roadsides, stacked pink-purple whorls of flowers
18.childFriendlyNote: Rub a horsemint leaf and sniff. It smells like lemon! The stacked purple flowers look like a tiny wedding cake

19.description: Firefly displays intensifying in humid areas, synchronized flashing in some eastern Texas woods
19.childFriendlyNote: The fireflies are putting on their best show (flash, flash, flash). They're talking to each other with light!

19.description: Baby bats being born in colonies, mothers returning from foraging to nurse in the dark
19.childFriendlyNote: Tiny pink baby bats cling upside-down waiting for mum. And she finds her baby among millions just by its voice and smell!

19.description: Horsemint at peak bloom, meadows and roadsides dotted with purple tiered flower towers
19.childFriendlyNote: Fields of stacked purple flowers smell lemony-fresh. Butterflies and bees are having a feast!

19.description: Painted buntings feeding chicks, parents making constant trips with caterpillars and seeds
19.childFriendlyNote: The rainbow dad brings bugs to his babies, back and forth, back and forth, all day long!

19.description: Texas spiny lizards hunting insects on tree trunks, quick dashes and freeze-frame stillness
19.childFriendlyNote: The big bumpy lizard runs up the tree. Stop! Runs again. Stop! It's playing a real-life game of freeze tag

20.description: Bat colonies at peak with nursing mothers, Austin's Congress Avenue Bridge emergence a must-see spectacle
20.childFriendlyNote: Stand on the bridge at sunset and watch a million bats swirl out. It takes 45 minutes for them all to leave!

20.description: Peak firefly season in eastern Texas, warm humid nights lit up with blinking yellow-green
20.childFriendlyNote: Catch a firefly gently in your cupped hands and peek through your fingers. Your hands glow like a magic lantern!

20.description: Scissor-tailed flycatcher chicks fledging, awkward juveniles with shorter tails learning to hawk insects
20.childFriendlyNote: Baby scissor-tails have stubby tails and keep missing the bugs. Practice makes perfect, little bird!

20.description: Roadrunners hunting lizards and snakes in brushy areas, running at top speed with prey dangling from bill
20.childFriendlyNote: The roadrunner sprints across the path with a lizard in its beak. Beep beep! (Well, it actually goes "coo-coo-coo")

20.description: Crape myrtle flower buds forming at branch tips, preparing for the long summer bloom
20.childFriendlyNote: Fat green buds are growing at the tips of the crape myrtle. They're going to pop into amazing crinkly flowers soon!

21.description: First crape myrtle blossoms opening in pink, purple, red and white, crinkly crepe-paper petals
21.childFriendlyNote: Crinkly flowers that feel like crepe paper are opening. Touch one gently, it's like a ruffled tissue-paper skirt!

21.description: Baby bats growing rapidly, clinging to cave and bridge ceilings while mothers forage
21.childFriendlyNote: Baby bats are getting furry now. They practice flapping their wings while hanging upside-down, getting ready to fly!

21.description: First cicadas of summer buzzing from tree canopies, their rising and falling drone becoming the sound of heat
21.childFriendlyNote: Bzzzzzzzzz, that loud rising buzz from the trees? That's a cicada, a big bug that lived underground for years and finally came up!

21.description: Painted bunting fledglings leaving nests, dull olive juveniles following parents through brush
21.childFriendlyNote: Baby painted buntings don't look like rainbows yet. They're plain green, like they forgot to put on their fancy clothes!

21.description: Roadrunner pairs raising chicks, parents sprinting with grasshoppers and small reptiles for hungry nestlings
21.childFriendlyNote: Mama roadrunner runs up with a big grasshopper. The babies fight over who gets the crunchy snack!

21.description: Turk's cap beginning to bloom, spiralled red flowers unfurling in shady garden spots
21.childFriendlyNote: Red flowers that never fully open. They stay twisted like a little turban, and hummingbirds love poking their beaks inside!

22.description: Crape myrtles blooming along streets and in yards, one of the few trees flowering in the heat
22.childFriendlyNote: When everything else is wilting, the crape myrtle shows off huge bunches of crinkly pink and purple flowers!

22.description: Cicada chorus building, empty brown shells clinging to tree bark where nymphs emerged
22.childFriendlyNote: Find a crunchy brown shell on a tree. A cicada climbed out of its old skin and left it behind like an empty spacesuit!

22.description: Young bats taking first flights, bat emergences at their most spectacular numbers
22.childFriendlyNote: The baby bats are learning to fly! Some wobble and loop, but they're getting better every night

22.description: Turk's cap in steady bloom, twisted red flowers attracting hummingbirds to shady garden corners
22.childFriendlyNote: The twisty red flowers are a hummingbird café. Watch the tiny birds zip in for a sip of nectar!

22.description: Green anoles hunting insects in the heat, turning brown on hot surfaces and green in shade
22.childFriendlyNote: Watch the anole change colour, green in the shade, brown in the sun! It's not a chameleon, but close!

23.description: Cicada drone at full volume, the defining soundtrack of Texas summer afternoons
23.childFriendlyNote: Close your eyes and listen. That loud bzzzzzz rising and falling is the sound of summer itself!

23.description: Crape myrtles in full glory, huge panicles of ruffled flowers in hot pink, lavender, red and white
23.childFriendlyNote: Crape myrtles are the queens of summer, big bunches of crinkly flowers when everything else is too hot to bloom!

23.description: Peak bat season, columns of 1.5 million bats spiraling from Austin's Congress Avenue Bridge at dusk
23.childFriendlyNote: The biggest bat show in the world! They eat 10,000 pounds of mosquitoes and moths every single night

23.description: Roadrunners panting in the heat with mouth agape, still hunting lizards and scorpions
23.childFriendlyNote: Even the roadrunner is hot. It stands in the shade panting, but still chases lizards when it spots one!

23.description: Turk's cap blooming steadily through the heat, red spiralled flowers in every shady garden corner
23.childFriendlyNote: Turk's cap just keeps blooming all summer. The hummingbirds say thank you!

24.description: Multiple cicada species calling, overlapping buzzes and clicks creating waves of sound in the heat
24.childFriendlyNote: Different cicadas make different sounds: some buzz, some click, some whine. It's a bug orchestra in the treetops!

24.description: Crape myrtles in sustained bloom, petals drifting down like coloured confetti on hot sidewalks
24.childFriendlyNote: Tiny crinkly petals fall like confetti on the sidewalk. Step on them and they feel like tissue paper

24.description: Scorpions active at night, glowing blue-green under UV light while hunting insects on walls and patios
24.childFriendlyNote: Shine a blacklight in the garden at night. Scorpions glow spooky blue-green! (Look but don't touch!)

24.description: Bat colonies at peak size, young bats now foraging independently alongside adults
24.childFriendlyNote: The teenage bats are hunting on their own now, swooping and diving after moths in the streetlights!

24.description: Texas spiny lizards laying eggs in warm soil, adults hunting in morning and evening to avoid midday heat
24.childFriendlyNote: The big spiny lizard only comes out in the cooler morning and evening now. It's too hot even for a lizard at noon!

25.description: Cicadas at peak volume, the relentless buzz the hallmark of brutal Texas summer heat
25.childFriendlyNote: The hotter it gets, the louder the cicadas buzz. They love the heat!

25.description: Crape myrtles continuing their long bloom, one of the only splashes of colour in the scorching landscape
25.childFriendlyNote: Everything looks dried up except the crape myrtle, still waving its crinkly flowers like colourful flags!

25.description: Massive bat emergences continuing at dusk, the dark ribbon visible against sunset skies
25.childFriendlyNote: The bats make a dark swirling river in the sunset sky. Hawks try to catch them but the bats are too quick!

25.description: Scorpions hunting nightly on warm surfaces, sometimes finding their way indoors seeking water
25.childFriendlyNote: Shake out your shoes in the morning. A scorpion might be hiding in there! They glow under blacklight

25.description: Turk's cap thriving in shade despite the heat, red flowers a vital nectar source for hummingbirds
25.childFriendlyNote: Turk's cap flowers are like little red swirly ice cream cones that hummingbirds stick their tongues into!

26.description: Cicada chorus peaking, their shed exoskeletons accumulating on tree trunks
26.childFriendlyNote: Collect the crunchy cicada shells off tree bark. They're like tiny perfect bug costumes left behind!

26.description: Crape myrtles at mid-summer peak, some trees covered in so many flowers the branches droop
26.childFriendlyNote: So many flowers the branches bend down like the tree is bowing to say "Look how beautiful I am!"

26.description: Bat colonies at their largest, consuming tonnes of agricultural pest insects nightly
26.childFriendlyNote: Each bat eats its own weight in bugs every night. Imagine eating your weight in pizza!

26.description: Roadrunners hunting in early morning before the heat, juveniles learning to chase prey
26.childFriendlyNote: Baby roadrunners are learning to hunt. They chase grasshoppers and sometimes trip over their own big feet!

26.description: Tiny hatchling anoles appearing on plants and fences, just a few centimetres long
26.childFriendlyNote: Teeny tiny baby lizards smaller than your pinky finger are popping up on the fence. They hatched all by themselves!

27.description: Cicadas buzzing from dawn to dusk, the loudest insects in North America at over 100 decibels
27.childFriendlyNote: Cicadas are as loud as a lawnmower! Cover your ears near a tree full of them, bzzzzzzzzz!

27.description: Crape myrtles still blooming strong through July heat, attracting pollinators
27.childFriendlyNote: The crape myrtle keeps going and going. It's the energizer bunny of summer flowers!

27.description: Peak bat season, all ages foraging, spectacular evening emergences from bridges and caves
27.childFriendlyNote: The bats are the best pest control: a whole colony eats enough bugs to fill a swimming pool every summer!

27.description: Peak scorpion activity on hot nights, females carrying babies on their backs
27.childFriendlyNote: Mama scorpion carries all her babies on her back, dozens of tiny scorpions riding piggyback! (Don't pick them up!)

27.description: Turk's cap blooming reliably through the heat, one of the best native plants for summer hummingbirds
27.childFriendlyNote: The red turk's cap flowers are the hummingbird's favourite summer restaurant, always open, always serving nectar!

28.description: Cicadas still at full chorus, dead adults littering sidewalks after completing their brief above-ground lives
28.childFriendlyNote: A cicada lived underground for years, then came up to sing for just a few weeks. What a wild life!

28.description: Crape myrtles pushing out new flower panicles as old ones fade, extending the bloom
28.childFriendlyNote: Just when one bunch of flowers fades, the crape myrtle grows new ones. It's like a flower machine!

28.description: Bat colonies still at peak, young bats fully independent and foraging far from roosts
28.childFriendlyNote: Teenage bats are expert flyers now. They zoom and dive catching moths with their echolocation superpowers!

28.description: Texas spiny lizards sheltering in shade during hottest hours, active at dawn and dusk
28.childFriendlyNote: Even the tough spiny lizard hides from the afternoon sun. Find them pressed flat against the shady side of trees

28.description: Roadrunners sunbathing in morning, spreading wings and fluffing back feathers to absorb warmth
28.childFriendlyNote: The roadrunner spreads its wings like a vampire cape and turns its back to the sun. It's solar-powered!

29.description: Late-season cicada species joining the chorus, slightly different buzz patterns in the canopy
29.childFriendlyNote: New cicadas with different songs are joining in. The summer concert has new performers!

29.description: Crape myrtles in sustained bloom, second and third flushes of flowers keeping trees colourful
29.childFriendlyNote: The crape myrtle has been blooming for two months and still going, what a champion!

29.description: Bat colonies beginning to thin slightly as some individuals start dispersing
29.childFriendlyNote: The bat show is still amazing, but a few bats are starting to head off on their own adventures

29.description: Multiple generations of anoles active, from tiny hatchlings to large territorial adults
29.childFriendlyNote: Big lizards, medium lizards, tiny baby lizards. The fence is like a lizard apartment building!

29.description: Turk's cap still flowering despite the heat, small red fruits beginning to form on older flowers
29.childFriendlyNote: Some turk's cap flowers are becoming little red berries. Birds will gobble them up later!

30.description: Cicada chorus still strong but beginning to thin in some areas as oldest individuals die off
30.childFriendlyNote: The cicada orchestra is still playing but some musicians are taking their final bow

30.description: Crape myrtles still blooming, seed pods forming on earlier flower clusters
30.childFriendlyNote: The crape myrtle has flowers and little round seed balls at the same time, multi-tasking tree!

30.description: Bat emergences still spectacular, colony sizes starting to decline as autumn migration approaches
30.childFriendlyNote: Still worth watching at sunset. The bat tornado swirls out but there are fewer bats each week now

30.description: Scorpions still active nightly, young scorpions now independent and hunting on their own
30.childFriendlyNote: Baby scorpions are on their own now, tiny but already glowing blue-green under a blacklight!

30.description: Texas sage erupting in purple blooms after summer rain, the "barometer bush" predicting storms
30.childFriendlyNote: After a rain, this silvery bush explodes with purple flowers overnight. People call it the rain sage because it knows when storms are coming!

31.description: Cicada chorus beginning to thin, late-season species still calling in afternoon heat
31.childFriendlyNote: The cicada buzz is getting quieter, fewer singers in the treetop choir each day

31.description: Late crape myrtle bloom, some trees still producing fresh flower clusters in August heat
31.childFriendlyNote: The crape myrtle is finally slowing down after months of blooming, what a marathon!

31.description: Texas sage blooming spectacularly after any summer rain, silvery bushes covered in purple
31.childFriendlyNote: Every time it rains, the silver bush turns purple like magic. Then the flowers fall off until the next rain!

31.description: Bat colonies thinning as some begin southward migration, evening flights still impressive
31.childFriendlyNote: Some bats are packing their invisible suitcases and heading to Mexico for winter!

31.description: Mockingbirds raising late broods, still singing vigorously from rooftops and power lines
31.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird is still singing at midnight. It never runs out of songs or energy!

32.description: Texas sage continuing to bloom after rain events, the barometer bush signalling moisture in the air
32.childFriendlyNote: If you see the sage bush covered in purple flowers, grab an umbrella. Rain is probably coming!

32.description: Cicada song fading, fewer individuals calling, end of the summer buzz approaching
32.childFriendlyNote: The cicada songs are getting quieter and lonelier. Summer is starting to wind down

32.description: Roadrunners fully grown with second brood fledglings, family groups hunting together
32.childFriendlyNote: A whole family of roadrunners sprints across the yard. The little ones run just as fast as the grown-ups!

32.description: Late-summer hatchling anoles abundant, tiny lizards hunting gnats on leaves and window screens
32.childFriendlyNote: Itty-bitty lizards hunt teeny-tiny bugs on the window screen. The whole world is a giant jungle to them!

32.description: Turk's cap still blooming in shade, red fruits ripening alongside fresh flowers
32.childFriendlyNote: The turk's cap has flowers and red berries at the same time: a shop that never closes for hummingbirds!

33.description: Texas sage reliably blooming after each rain event through late summer
33.childFriendlyNote: Rain comes, purple flowers appear, like clockwork! The sage bush is nature's weather reporter

33.description: Mockingbirds completing final broods, juveniles practising their own songs with rough imitations
33.childFriendlyNote: Young mockingbirds are trying to copy sounds but keep getting mixed up. It's like listening to a kid learning to whistle!

33.description: Late-summer monarchs building up before fall migration, caterpillars on late milkweed
33.childFriendlyNote: Monarch caterpillars are munching milkweed as fast as they can. They need to grow up and fly to Mexico!

33.description: Bat numbers declining as migration accelerates, but evening flights still notable
33.childFriendlyNote: Fewer bats under the bridge each week. They're flying south to warmer caves in Mexico

33.description: Prickly pear tunas (fruit) turning from green to reddish-purple, attracting birds and mammals
33.childFriendlyNote: The cactus fruits are turning purple-red. Birds love eating them and their poop turns bright pink!

34.description: Super-generation monarchs emerging, the special butterflies that will make the long flight to Mexico
34.childFriendlyNote: These are special monarchs. They won't lay eggs, they'll fly 2,000 miles to Mexico and live for 8 months!

34.description: Texas sage responding to late summer storms with reliable purple blooming
34.childFriendlyNote: The rain prophet bush is still doing its thing, purple flowers after every storm!

34.description: Last clutches of anole eggs hatching, the tiniest hatchlings of the year appearing on plant stems
34.childFriendlyNote: The last batch of baby lizards for the year, so tiny they can sit on a penny!

34.description: Prickly pear fruit ripening to deep magenta, mockingbirds and woodpeckers feeding on them
34.childFriendlyNote: Ripe cactus fruit is so purple it stains everything. Birds eat it and fly away with purple beaks!

34.description: Crape myrtle bloom finally winding down, seed capsules forming in clusters
34.childFriendlyNote: The crape myrtle's long flower party is ending. Little round seed balls are taking the flowers' place

35.description: Monarch fall migration beginning, first butterflies heading south through Texas
35.childFriendlyNote: The great monarch journey south has started. Watch for orange butterflies all heading the same direction!

35.description: Goldenrod beginning to bloom along roadsides and meadow edges, bright yellow plumes
35.childFriendlyNote: Golden yellow feathery flowers are popping up along the road. They look like nature's cheerleader pom-poms!

35.description: Cardinals moulting into fresh plumage, some males looking patchy with new and old feathers
35.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal looks a bit scruffy. It's losing old feathers and growing shiny new ones, like getting a new outfit!

35.description: Texas sage continuing its rain-triggered bloom cycle through the last weeks of summer
35.childFriendlyNote: Purple blooms after the rain, every single time. The sage bush never gets it wrong!

35.description: Turk's cap ramping up bloom as summer heat begins easing, bright red fruits ripening
35.childFriendlyNote: The turk's cap is blooming even more now. It saved its best show for the end of summer!

36.description: Monarch migration building, more butterflies moving south through Texas each day
36.childFriendlyNote: More monarchs are flying south every day. They ride the wind like tiny orange gliders heading to Mexico!

36.description: Goldenrod in full bloom, meadows and roadsides glowing golden yellow
36.childFriendlyNote: Fields of gold! The goldenrod turns meadows into a yellow sea. And butterflies are having a nectar party!

36.description: Fall asters beginning to bloom in purple and blue, brightening dry autumn landscapes
36.childFriendlyNote: Little purple daisy-like flowers are popping up everywhere. They look like tiny stars that fell into the grass!

36.description: Ruby-throated hummingbirds fuelling up before southward migration, aggressively defending feeders
36.childFriendlyNote: The hummingbirds are eating extra today. They need to get fat before flying across the entire Gulf of Mexico!

36.description: Mockingbirds quieter now, saving energy after a long breeding season of constant singing
36.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird is taking a singing break. Even the best musicians need a rest!

37.description: Peak monarch migration through Texas, hundreds visible nectaring on goldenrod and frostweed
37.childFriendlyNote: So many monarchs! Some bushes have dozens of orange butterflies all resting and sipping. It's monarch highway!

37.description: Goldenrod at peak bloom, vital nectar source for migrating monarchs and other pollinators
37.childFriendlyNote: The golden flowers are like petrol stations for butterflies. Stop, fill up, and keep flying south!

37.description: Fall asters in full bloom, purple-blue flowers providing late-season nectar for butterflies and bees
37.childFriendlyNote: Purple star-flowers and golden plumes side by side. Autumn is painting the meadow in purple and gold!

37.description: Beautyberry clusters turning vivid magenta-purple, bright berries hugging the stems
37.childFriendlyNote: Bright purple berry clusters wrap around the stems like purple bubble necklaces. They're almost too purple to be real!

37.description: Texas sage responding to early autumn moisture, beautiful against the golden landscape
37.childFriendlyNote: The silver bush puts on its purple dress one more time before autumn really arrives

38.description: Monarch migration at peak intensity through central Texas, massive roosts forming in trees at night
38.childFriendlyNote: At night, monarchs huddle together in trees. A single tree can hold thousands, dripping with orange wings!

38.description: Beautyberry at peak colour, electric purple berry clusters unmistakable in woodland understory
38.childFriendlyNote: These berries are so purple they look like someone painted them with a marker. Birds feast on them like candy!

38.description: Goldenrod still blooming, providing crucial fuel for southbound monarchs
38.childFriendlyNote: The goldenrod flowers are fading but still feeding the last wave of travelling monarchs

38.description: Fall asters continuing to bloom, one of the last wildflower shows of the year
38.childFriendlyNote: The purple asters are still open when most other flowers have gone to sleep for the year

38.description: Pecan nuts beginning to fill out in their green husks, weighing down branch tips
38.childFriendlyNote: The pecan tree's branches are bending with heavy green nuts. Inside each one is the yummy nut we eat in pie!

39.description: Monarch migration still strong, late-September waves of butterflies streaming south on north winds
39.childFriendlyNote: When a cool front blows in from the north, it pushes the monarchs south like orange leaves on the wind!

39.description: Beautyberry clusters being eaten by mockingbirds, cardinals, and armadillos
39.childFriendlyNote: The birds discovered the purple berries. They're disappearing fast! Even armadillos eat the ones that fall

39.description: Pecan husks beginning to split, revealing the smooth brown shell underneath
39.childFriendlyNote: The green jackets on the pecans are cracking open. You can see the smooth brown nut peeking out!

39.description: Fall asters fading, seed heads forming with fluffy white pappus ready to drift on the wind
39.childFriendlyNote: The purple flowers are turning into little fluffy parachutes. Blow on them and watch the seeds fly away!

39.description: Cardinals in fresh plumage after moult, vivid red males bright against turning foliage
39.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal got all its new feathers. It's the brightest red you've ever seen, like a flying tomato!

40.description: Late monarch migration, final waves passing through Texas on their way to Mexican mountain forests
40.childFriendlyNote: The last monarchs are hurrying south. Wave goodbye, they have mountains to reach before winter!

40.description: Pecans beginning to fall, squirrels and crows competing to gather the first nuts
40.childFriendlyNote: Pecans are raining down (bonk!) squirrels grab them and run, stuffing their cheeks like furry shopping bags!

40.description: Beautyberry clusters thinning as birds strip them, bright purple still visible among fading leaves
40.childFriendlyNote: The birds have eaten most of the purple berries but a few clusters still glow in the fading leaves

40.description: Cardinals beginning to form loose winter flocks, visiting feeders in small groups
40.childFriendlyNote: Cardinals are teaming up for winter. A whole gang of red birds at the feeder is called a "conclave"!

40.description: Texas sage giving late autumn blooms after October rains, purple flowers on silvery foliage
40.childFriendlyNote: One last burst of purple from the rain sage. Autumn rains bring autumn flowers!

41.description: Peak pecan harvest, nuts falling heavily and covering ground beneath trees
41.childFriendlyNote: Fill your pockets with pecans! Crack one open and eat the sweet nutty insides: nature's candy!

41.description: Last straggling monarchs passing through, migration nearly complete for the year
41.childFriendlyNote: The very last monarchs flutter past. See you next spring, little travellers!

41.description: First cedar waxwing flocks returning for winter, high thin calls overhead as they seek berries
41.childFriendlyNote: The sleek masked birds are back for winter! They travel in noisy flocks making soft "seee-seee" calls

41.description: Mockingbirds establishing winter berry territories, aggressively defending holly and pyracantha bushes
41.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird picks its favourite berry bush and chases every other bird away: "My berries! All mine!"

41.description: Green anoles slowing down, basking on warm afternoons but increasingly retreating to shelter
41.childFriendlyNote: The lizards are getting sleepy. They only come out on the warmest afternoons for a quick sunbathe

42.description: Pecan harvest continuing, golden-yellow leaves beginning to fall from the trees
42.childFriendlyNote: Pecan trees are dropping nuts and golden leaves at the same time. It's raining treasure!

42.description: Cedar waxwing flocks growing, descending on fruiting trees in chattering groups
42.childFriendlyNote: A whole flock of waxwings lands in the holly tree. They strip every red berry in minutes flat!

42.description: Cardinals gathering in larger winter groups, bright red males vivid against autumn browns
42.childFriendlyNote: Red cardinals against brown autumn leaves. It's like nature arranged the colours on purpose!

42.description: Armadillos busy foraging through leaf litter in the pleasant autumn weather, leaving small divots in lawns
42.childFriendlyNote: The armoured digger is making little holes in the yard. It's sniffing out juicy grubs under the leaves!

42.description: Live oaks standing green and full while other trees turn and drop leaves around them
42.childFriendlyNote: All the other trees are losing their leaves but the live oak is still green. It never quits!

43.description: Late pecan harvest, trees dropping the last nuts and shedding butter-yellow leaves
43.childFriendlyNote: The pecan trees are nearly empty. Grab the last ones before the squirrels do!

43.description: First sandhill cranes arriving from the north, their bugling calls heard overhead as V-formations pass
43.childFriendlyNote: Listen! A rattling trumpet sound from the sky. Look up and see huge grey birds flying in a V, coming to spend winter!

43.description: Cedar waxwings well established, roving flocks moving between fruiting trees across the region
43.childFriendlyNote: The waxwings are settling in for winter. Watch them pass berries to each other beak-to-beak. So polite!

43.description: Mockingbirds fiercely guarding winter berry territories, chasing robins and waxwings away
43.childFriendlyNote: The mockingbird guard sits on the holly bush all day long. Get away from my berries, it says to every bird!

43.description: Cardinals visiting feeders more frequently as natural food diminishes, whistling softly
43.childFriendlyNote: The red cardinal taps at the bird feeder: "Please sir, may I have some more seeds?"

44.description: Sandhill cranes settling into winter grounds, flocks gathering in agricultural fields and wetlands
44.childFriendlyNote: Hundreds of tall grey cranes stand in the field like a feathery army. They honk and dance and strut around!

44.description: Cedar waxwings feasting on late-season berries, possumhaw holly a favourite
44.childFriendlyNote: The waxwings found a tree full of red berries and they are not sharing, eating every single one!

44.description: Wintering robin flocks returning, large groups foraging in pecan leaf litter and berry trees
44.childFriendlyNote: The robin army is back for winter! They flip leaves with their beaks looking for worms, flip, flip, tug!

44.description: Live oaks green and unchanging while deciduous trees stand bare, acorns still falling
44.childFriendlyNote: The live oak is the toughest tree in Texas, stays green no matter what, while every other tree goes bare!

44.description: Armadillos active on mild autumn evenings, rooting energetically through garden beds
44.childFriendlyNote: The armadillo is digging up the flower bed again, snuffle snuffle dig dig, looking for buried bugs!

45.description: Sandhill cranes established in wintering areas, spectacular dancing displays in open fields
45.childFriendlyNote: The cranes dance! They bow, jump, flap their wings, and throw sticks in the air. It's a crane ballet!

45.description: Large cedar waxwing flocks stripping berry-laden trees across urban and rural areas
45.childFriendlyNote: A tree full of berries in the morning can be completely stripped by waxwings before lunch, fast eaters!

45.description: Robin winter flocks growing, gathering in large roosts at dusk and dispersing at dawn to forage
45.childFriendlyNote: At sunset, thousands of robins fly to the same group of trees for a big sleepover, safety in numbers!

45.description: Cardinals in winter flocks of up to a dozen, bright against bare branches and grey skies
45.childFriendlyNote: A flock of red cardinals in a bare tree looks like the tree grew ornaments, living Christmas decorations!

45.description: Red-tailed hawks soaring over bare fields, easier to spot now that leaves have fallen
45.childFriendlyNote: With the leaves gone, you can finally see the hawk nests high in the trees, and the hawks circling above!

46.description: Sandhill cranes in full winter residence, bugling calls echoing across agricultural fields at dawn
46.childFriendlyNote: The cranes wake up at dawn and shout their crazy trumpet call across the fields: garoooo-a-a-a!

46.description: Cedar waxwings everywhere, their thin high-pitched whistle a constant winter soundtrack
46.childFriendlyNote: Hear that thin "seeeee" sound from the treetop? A whole flock of masked berry-thieves is up there!

46.description: Cardinals brightening the dull November landscape, singing occasional clear whistles on warmer mornings
46.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal is the brightest thing in the whole garden now that the flowers are gone, a little red flame!

46.description: Huge robin flocks foraging in open areas, sometimes numbering in the thousands
46.childFriendlyNote: So many robins on the playing field you can't count them all. They're like a feathery carpet that walks!

46.description: Live oaks still fully green, providing vital shelter and food for winter birds
46.childFriendlyNote: The live oak is like a green umbrella in a brown world. Birds hide in its leaves to stay warm and safe

47.description: Male Ashe juniper cones maturing, brown-gold pollen cones getting ready for December release
47.childFriendlyNote: The juniper trees are loading up their pollen cannons. Golden-brown cones are getting fat and ready to burst!

47.description: Sandhill cranes well settled in winter territories, family groups with cinnamon-brown juveniles
47.childFriendlyNote: Baby cranes are brown and fuzzy while mum and dad are grey. Can you spot which is the kid?

47.description: Cedar waxwings in peak winter numbers, roving flocks cleaning out berry trees one by one
47.childFriendlyNote: The waxwing flock moves like a team. They find a berry tree, eat everything, then zoom to the next one!

47.description: Robin flocks occupying hackberry and holly trees, gorging on winter berries
47.childFriendlyNote: The robins eat so many hackberries their chests turn orangey-red: berry-powered birds!

47.description: Cardinals frequenting feeders in the cooling weather, paired birds often visiting together
47.childFriendlyNote: Mr and Mrs Cardinal come to the feeder together. He's red and she's golden-brown, a beautiful pair!

48.description: Ashe juniper pollen cones nearly mature, first early releases possible on warm dry days
48.childFriendlyNote: The juniper trees are about to start their big sneeze. The golden pollen cones are getting ready to poof!

48.description: Sandhill cranes dancing in winter fields, their courtship displays beginning even in late November
48.childFriendlyNote: Even in winter the cranes dance, leaping high, wings spread, like they're celebrating something!

48.description: Cedar waxwings working through holly and juniper berries, feeding heavily in short winter days
48.childFriendlyNote: The waxwings eat and eat all day. Winter days are short so they have to fill up fast before dark!

48.description: Cardinals at feeders and in berry bushes, a splash of red cheer in the late autumn landscape
48.childFriendlyNote: Nothing cheers up a grey November day like a bright red cardinal at your window, hello, feathered friend!

48.description: Great blue herons stalking winter ponds and creeks, standing perfectly still in the cold water
48.childFriendlyNote: The tall grey-blue bird stands so still in the creek that fish swim right past. Then stab! Got one!

49.description: Cedar fever season beginning in earnest, first significant pollen releases from Ashe juniper
49.childFriendlyNote: The junipers are starting to puff yellow clouds again. Here comes the big sneeze season!

49.description: Sandhill cranes in winter flocks, their prehistoric bugling calls carrying across fields at dawn
49.childFriendlyNote: The cranes have been around since dinosaur times. Their call sounds like it comes from a million years ago!

49.description: Cardinals in their most vivid winter plumage, frequently visiting feeders in the early December chill
49.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal's red feathers glow even brighter in December, like a tiny fire in the cold grey garden

49.description: Cedar waxwings in large flocks, their sleek silhouettes and thin calls a constant winter presence
49.childFriendlyNote: The berry-eating bandits with their cool black masks are everywhere. They travel in a big hungry gang!

49.description: Robin winter flocks established, thousands roosting together in sheltered groves at night
49.childFriendlyNote: At bedtime, robins gather in one big tree. Imagine a sleepover with a thousand friends!

50.description: Cedar pollen increasing rapidly, visible yellow haze on Hill Country mornings
50.childFriendlyNote: Look at the hills in the morning. A yellow haze hangs in the air! That's millions of tiny pollen grains from the junipers

50.description: Cardinals joining mixed winter flocks at feeders with sparrows, juncos, and titmice
50.childFriendlyNote: The bird feeder is like a December party: cardinals, sparrows, and titmice all eating together!

50.description: Sandhill cranes wintering peacefully, family groups feeding together in harvested fields
50.childFriendlyNote: Crane families stick together all winter: mum, dad, and the teenager eating corn in the field together

50.description: Great horned owls beginning courtship duets, male and female hooting back and forth at dusk
50.childFriendlyNote: Listen at dusk. Two owls hoot back and forth like a love song! "Hoo-hoo-hoo" says he. "Hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo" says she!

50.description: Live oaks still fully green, acorns mostly gone, providing winter shelter for birds
50.childFriendlyNote: The live oak is the only tree on the street still wearing its green outfit. It never takes it off!

51.description: Cedar fever ramping up, pollen counts rising daily as more male trees begin releasing
51.childFriendlyNote: More and more juniper trees are joining the pollen party. The yellow clouds are getting bigger every day!

51.description: Great horned owl pairs calling to each other in the long December nights, preparing to nest
51.childFriendlyNote: The owl couple hoots in the dark December night. They're picking out a nest spot before everyone else even thinks about babies!

51.description: Cedar waxwings feasting on juniper berries, holly berries, and any remaining fruit
51.childFriendlyNote: The waxwings eat the juniper berries that give them their name: cedar waxwings eating cedar berries!

51.description: Cardinals brightening the December landscape, a beloved backyard sight during the holidays
51.childFriendlyNote: Red cardinals in green holly bushes look just like Christmas cards, nature's holiday decorations!

51.description: Sandhill cranes continuing winter routines, flying between roost sites and feeding fields daily
51.childFriendlyNote: Every morning the cranes fly from their sleeping pond to the feeding field, and every evening they fly back, like a commute!

52.description: Cedar fever in full swing, massive pollen clouds visible drifting from Hill Country juniper groves
52.childFriendlyNote: The junipers are going all out. Golden pollen smoke drifts between the hills like a yellow fog!

52.description: Cardinals visiting feeders on cold December mornings, bright red against grey winter skies
52.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal waits on a branch for its turn at the feeder, patient and glowing red like a tiny holiday light

52.description: Great horned owls selecting nest sites, some females already settling in to lay eggs
52.childFriendlyNote: While everyone celebrates the holidays, the great horned owl is already sitting on eggs, the earliest nesting bird around!

52.description: Cedar waxwings in large flocks, a constant presence at berry trees through the holiday season
52.childFriendlyNote: The waxwings are having their own holiday feast. Every berry tree is their dinner table!

52.description: Sandhill cranes settled into winter routine, their ancient rattling calls ringing across cold fields
52.childFriendlyNote: The cranes will be here all winter, dancing and trumpeting. They're the best winter visitors in Texas!

52.description: Live oaks steadfastly green as the year closes, unchanged through every season
52.childFriendlyNote: The live oak ends the year the same way it started: green, strong, and full of leaves. What a tree!
